questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: One mole of diatomic gas having rotational modes only is kept in a cylinder with a piston system. The cross-section area of the cylinder is $4$ cm$^2$. The gas is heated slowly to raise the temperature by $1.2\,^\circ$C during which the piston moves by $25$ mm. The amount of heat supplied to the gas is ________ J. (Atmospheric pressure $=100$ kPa, $R=8.3$ J/mol·K) (Neglect mass of the piston)
questions.solution:
Using the first law of thermodynamics:
$Q = \Delta U + W$

Since the gas is diatomic with rotational modes only, the degrees of freedom are $f = 5$, so:
$C_V = \dfrac{5}{2}R$

For $n = 1\text{ mole}$ and $\Delta T = 1.2\text{ K}$:
$\Delta U = nC_V\Delta T = 1 \times \dfrac{5}{2} \times 8.3 \times 1.2 = 24.9\text{ J}$

Work done by the gas:
$W = P\,\Delta V$

Cross-sectional area of the piston:
$A = 4\text{ cm}^2 = 4 \times 10^{-4}\text{ m}^2$

Piston displacement:
$x = 25\text{ mm} = 2.5 \times 10^{-2}\text{ m}$

Change in volume:
$\Delta V = A \cdot x = (4 \times 10^{-4})(2.5 \times 10^{-2}) = 1 \times 10^{-5}\text{ m}^3$

With $P = 100\text{ kPa} = 10^5\text{ Pa}$:
$W = (10^5)(1 \times 10^{-5}) = 1\text{ J}$

Therefore, the heat supplied is:
$Q = \Delta U + W = 24.9 + 1 = 25.9\text{ J}$

Hence, the heat supplied to the gas is $25.9\text{ J}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Initial pressure and volume of a monoatomic ideal gas are $P$ and $V$. The change in internal energy of this gas in adiabatic expansion to volume $V_{final}=27V$ is ________ J.
questions.solution:
For a monoatomic ideal gas, the ratio of specific heats is $\gamma = \dfrac{5}{3}$.

In an adiabatic process, $PV^{\gamma} = \text{constant}$.

$P_1 V_1^{\gamma} = P_2 V_2^{\gamma}$

$P V^{5/3} = P_2 (27V)^{5/3}$

$P_2 = P \left(\dfrac{1}{27}\right)^{5/3} = \dfrac{P}{243}$

The change in internal energy is given by:

$\Delta U = \dfrac{P_2 V_2 - P_1 V_1}{\gamma - 1}$

Substituting the values:

$\Delta U = \dfrac{\left(\dfrac{P}{243}\right)(27V) - PV}{\dfrac{5}{3} - 1}$

$\Delta U = \dfrac{\dfrac{PV}{9} - PV}{\dfrac{2}{3}}$

$\Delta U = \dfrac{-\dfrac{8}{9}PV}{\dfrac{2}{3}} = -\dfrac{4}{3}PV$

Answer: $-\dfrac{4}{3}PV$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A cylinder with adiabatic walls is closed at both ends and is divided into two compartments by a frictionless adiabatic piston. Ideal gas is filled in both (left and right) the compartments at same $P, V, T$. Heating is started from left side until pressure changes to $\dfrac{27P}{8}$. If initial volume of each compartment was $9$ litres then the final volume in right-hand side compartment is __________ litres. (for this ideal gas $C_P/C_V = 1.5$)
questions.solution:
The right compartment is enclosed by adiabatic walls and an adiabatic piston, and no heat is supplied to it. Therefore, the gas in the right compartment undergoes an adiabatic compression.

Since the piston is frictionless, the pressure in the right compartment is always equal to the pressure in the left compartment. The final pressure in both compartments is $P_f = \dfrac{27P}{8}$.

For the adiabatic process in the right compartment, the equation is:
$P_i V_i^\gamma = P_f V_f^\gamma$

Given $P_i = P$, $V_i = 9$ L, $P_f = \dfrac{27P}{8}$, and $\gamma = \dfrac{C_P}{C_V} = 1.5 = \dfrac{3}{2}$. Substituting these values:
$P(9)^{3/2} = \left(\dfrac{27P}{8}\right) V_f^{3/2}$

Since $9^{3/2} = (3^2)^{3/2} = 3^3 = 27$, the equation becomes:
$27P = \dfrac{27P}{8} V_f^{3/2}$

Dividing both sides by $27P$:
$1 = \dfrac{1}{8} V_f^{3/2}$

$V_f^{3/2} = 8$

Taking the power of $2/3$ on both sides:
$V_f = (8)^{2/3} = (2^3)^{2/3} = 2^2 = 4$ litres.

Answer: $4$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two closed vessels of same volume are joined through a narrow tube and both vessels are filled with air of pressure $90$ kPa and temperature $400$ K. Keeping the temperature of one vessel constant at $400$ K the second vessel temperature is raised to $500$ K. The final pressure in the vessels is _______ kPa.
questions.solution:
Let the volume of each vessel be $V$.

Initially, both vessels are at pressure $P_1 = 90$ kPa and temperature $T_1 = 400$ K.

Total number of moles initially is given by:

$n_i = \dfrac{P_1 V}{R T_1} + \dfrac{P_1 V}{R T_1} = \dfrac{2 P_1 V}{R T_1}$

Finally, the temperature of the first vessel is $T_1 = 400$ K and the second vessel is $T_2 = 500$ K. Let the final pressure be $P_f$.

Total number of moles finally is given by:

$n_f = \dfrac{P_f V}{R T_1} + \dfrac{P_f V}{R T_2}$

Since the total number of moles remains constant, $n_i = n_f$:

$\dfrac{2 P_1 V}{R T_1} = \dfrac{P_f V}{R T_1} + \dfrac{P_f V}{R T_2}$

Substituting the given values:

$\dfrac{2 \times 90}{400} = \dfrac{P_f}{400} + \dfrac{P_f}{500}$

$\dfrac{180}{400} = P_f \left( \dfrac{1}{400} + \dfrac{1}{500} \right)$

$\dfrac{180}{400} = P_f \left( \dfrac{5 + 4}{2000} \right)$

$\dfrac{180}{400} = P_f \left( \dfrac{9}{2000} \right)$

$P_f = \dfrac{180 \times 2000}{400 \times 9}$

$P_f = 20 \times 5 = 100$ kPa

Answer: $100$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A certain gas is isothermally compressed to $\left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right)^{rd}$ of its initial volume ($V_o = 3$ litre) by applying required pressure. If the bulk modulus of the gas is $3 \times 10^5$ N/m$^2$, the magnitude of work done on the gas is _______ J.
questions.solution:
For an isothermal process, the isothermal bulk modulus equals the gas pressure:
$B_T = -V\dfrac{dP}{dV}$

Since $PV = \text{constant}$, differentiating gives $P\,dV + V\,dP = 0$, so $\dfrac{dP}{dV} = -\dfrac{P}{V}$, which yields $B_T = P$.

Therefore, the initial pressure is:
$P_o = 3 \times 10^5\text{ N/m}^2$

Volumes:
$V_o = 3\text{ L} = 3 \times 10^{-3}\text{ m}^3$
$V_f = \dfrac{1}{3}V_o = 10^{-3}\text{ m}^3$

Work done on the gas during an isothermal compression:
$W_{\text{on}} = -W_{\text{by}} = -P_o V_o \ln\left(\dfrac{V_f}{V_o}\right) = P_o V_o \ln\left(\dfrac{V_o}{V_f}\right)$

$W_{\text{on}} = (3 \times 10^5)(3 \times 10^{-3})\ln 3$

$W_{\text{on}} = 900 \ln 3\text{ J}$

Using $\ln 3 \approx 1.0986$:
$W_{\text{on}} \approx 900 \times 1.0986 \approx 988.74\text{ J}$

Rounded to the nearest integer:
$W_{\text{on}} \approx 989\text{ J}$

Hence, the work done on the gas is approximately $989\text{ J}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: An ideal gas at pressure $P$ and temperature $T$ is expanding such that $PT^3 = $ constant. The coefficient of volume expansion of the gas is _______.
questions.solution:
Given the process equation for the ideal gas:

$PT^3 = \text{constant}$

From the ideal gas equation, $PV = nRT$, which gives $P = \dfrac{nRT}{V}$.

Substituting $P$ into the process equation:

$\left(\dfrac{nRT}{V}\right) T^3 = \text{constant}$

$\dfrac{T^4}{V} = \text{constant}$

$V = k T^4$

Differentiating both sides with respect to temperature $T$:

$\dfrac{dV}{dT} = 4k T^3$

The coefficient of volume expansion $\gamma$ is defined as:

$\gamma = \dfrac{1}{V} \dfrac{dV}{dT}$

Substituting the values of $V and \dfrac{dV}{dT}$:

$\gamma = \dfrac{1}{k T^4} (4k T^3) = \dfrac{4}{T}$

Answer: $\dfrac{4}{T}$
questions.question: An ideal gas at pressure $P$ and temperature $T$ is expanding such that $PT^3 = $ constant. The coefficient of volume expansion of the gas is _______.

The coefficient of volume expansion $\gamma$ is defined as:

$\gamma = \dfrac{1}{V} \dfrac{dV}{dT}$

Substituting the values of $V and \dfrac{dV}{dT}$:

$\gamma = \dfrac{1}{k T^4} (4k T^3) = \dfrac{4}{T}$

Answer: $\dfrac{4}{T}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
Consider the following statements:
A. Zeroth law of thermodynamics gives concept of temperature
B. First law of thermodynamics gives concept of internal energy
C. In isothermal expansion of ideal gas, $\Delta Q \neq \Delta W$
D. Product of intensive and extensive variables is extensive
E. The ratio of any extensive variable to mass will be an extensive variable
Choose the correct combination of statements from the options given below:
questions.solution:
Statement A is correct because the zeroth law of thermodynamics defines temperature and thermal equilibrium.

Statement B is correct because the first law of thermodynamics introduces the concept of internal energy through the equation $\Delta Q = \Delta U + \Delta W$.

Statement C is incorrect because for an isothermal expansion of an ideal gas, the change in internal energy $\Delta U = 0$. According to the first law of thermodynamics, $\Delta Q = \Delta W$.

Statement D is correct because if an intensive variable (which is independent of the size of the system) is multiplied by an extensive variable (which is directly proportional to the size of the system), the product will be directly proportional to the size of the system, making it an extensive variable.

Statement E is incorrect because the ratio of two extensive variables (like any extensive variable and mass) is independent of the size of the system, making it an intensive variable.

Therefore, only statements A, B, and D are correct.

Answer: A, B and D Only

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: An ideal gas undergoes a process maintaining relation between pressure $(P)$ and volume $(V)$ as $P = P_o\left(1 + \left(\dfrac{V_o}{V}\right)^2\right)^{-1}$, where $P_o$ and $V_o$ are constants. If two samples $A$ and $B$ (two moles each) with initial volumes $V_o$ and $3V_o$ respectively undergo above mentioned process and attain same pressure, then the difference at the temperatures of these samples, $T_B - T_A$ is _____. ($R = $ gas constant)
questions.solution:
The given relation between pressure and volume is:

$P = P_o\left(1 + \left(\dfrac{V_o}{V}\right)^2\right)^{-1}$

For sample A, the initial volume is $V_A = V_o$. Substituting this into the given relation, the initial pressure $P_A$ is:

$P_A = P_o\left(1 + \left(\dfrac{V_o}{V_o}\right)^2\right)^{-1} = \dfrac{P_o}{2}$

Using the ideal gas equation $PV = nRT$ for $n = 2$ moles, the initial temperature $T_A$ is:

$T_A = \dfrac{P_A V_A}{nR} = \dfrac{\left(\dfrac{P_o}{2}\right) V_o}{2R} = \dfrac{P_o V_o}{4R}$

For sample B, the initial volume is $V_B = 3V_o$. Substituting this into the relation, the initial pressure $P_B$ is:

$P_B = P_o\left(1 + \left(\dfrac{V_o}{3V_o}\right)^2\right)^{-1} = P_o\left(1 + \dfrac{1}{9}\right)^{-1} = \dfrac{9P_o}{10}$

The initial temperature $T_B$ for $n = 2$ moles is:

$T_B = \dfrac{P_B V_B}{nR} = \dfrac{\left(\dfrac{9P_o}{10}\right) (3V_o)}{2R} = \dfrac{27P_o V_o}{20R}$

The difference in the initial temperatures of the two samples is:

$T_B - T_A = \dfrac{27P_o V_o}{20R} - \dfrac{P_o V_o}{4R}$

$T_B - T_A = \dfrac{27P_o V_o - 5P_o V_o}{20R} = \dfrac{22P_o V_o}{20R} = \dfrac{11P_o V_o}{10R}$

Answer: $\dfrac{11P_o V_o}{10R}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: $5$ moles of unknown gas is heated at constant volume from $10 \, °C$ to $20 \, °C$. The molar specific heat of this gas at constant pressure $c_p = 8$ cal/mol.°C and $R = 8.36$ J/mol.°C. The change in the internal energy of the gas is _______ calorie.
questions.solution:
Given $n = 5$ moles, $\Delta T = 20^{\circ}\text{C} - 10^{\circ}\text{C} = 10^{\circ}\text{C}$.

The molar specific heat at constant pressure is $c_p = 8 \text{ cal/mol}\cdot^{\circ}\text{C}$.

The universal gas constant is $R = 8.36 \text{ J/mol}\cdot^{\circ}\text{C}$.

Converting $R$ into calories, we use $1 \text{ cal} = 4.18 \text{ J}$:

$R = \dfrac{8.36}{4.18} \text{ cal/mol}\cdot^{\circ}\text{C} = 2 \text{ cal/mol}\cdot^{\circ}\text{C}$

Using Mayer's relation, the molar specific heat at constant volume is:

$c_v = c_p - R = 8 - 2 = 6 \text{ cal/mol}\cdot^{\circ}\text{C}$

The change in internal energy of the gas is given by:

$\Delta U = n c_v \Delta T$

$\Delta U = 5 \times 6 \times 10 = 300 \text{ cal}$

Answer: $300$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Heat is supplied to a diatomic gas at constant pressure. Then the ratio of $\Delta Q : \Delta U : \Delta W$ is _______.
questions.solution:
For a diatomic gas, the number of degrees of freedom is $f = 5$.

The molar heat capacity at constant volume is $C_v = \dfrac{f}{2}R = \dfrac{5}{2}R$.

The molar heat capacity at constant pressure is $C_p = C_v + R = \dfrac{7}{2}R$.

At constant pressure, the heat supplied is $\Delta Q = nC_p\Delta T = n\left(\dfrac{7}{2}R\right)\Delta T$.

The change in internal energy is $\Delta U = nC_v\Delta T = n\left(\dfrac{5}{2}R\right)\Delta T$.

The work done by the gas is $\Delta W = nR\Delta T = n\left(\dfrac{2}{2}R\right)\Delta T$.

The ratio $\Delta Q : \Delta U : \Delta W$ is $\dfrac{7}{2} : \dfrac{5}{2} : \dfrac{2}{2} = 7 : 5 : 2$.

Answer: $7 : 5 : 2$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A vessel contains $0.15$ m$^3$ of a gas at pressure $8$ bar and temperature $140°$C with $c_p = 3R$ and $c_v = 2R$. It is expanded adiabatically till pressure falls to $1$ bar. The work done during this process is _______ kJ. ($R$ is gas constant)
questions.solution:
Given $P_1 = 8$ bar $= 8 \times 10^5$ Pa, $V_1 = 0.15$ m$^3$, and $P_2 = 1$ bar $= 10^5$ Pa.

The adiabatic index $\gamma$ is given by:

$\gamma = \dfrac{c_p}{c_v} = \dfrac{3R}{2R} = 1.5$

For an adiabatic process, $P_1 V_1^\gamma = P_2 V_2^\gamma$.

$V_2 = V_1 \left( \dfrac{P_1}{P_2} \right)^{\dfrac{1}{\gamma}}$

$V_2 = 0.15 \times \left( \dfrac{8}{1} \right)^{\dfrac{1}{1.5}} = 0.15 \times 8^{\dfrac{2}{3}} = 0.15 \times 4 = 0.6$ m$^3$

The work done during the adiabatic expansion is:

$W = \dfrac{P_1 V_1 - P_2 V_2}{\gamma - 1}$

$W = \dfrac{8 \times 10^5 \times 0.15 - 1 \times 10^5 \times 0.6}{1.5 - 1}$

$W = \dfrac{1.2 \times 10^5 - 0.6 \times 10^5}{0.5}$

$W = \dfrac{0.6 \times 10^5}{0.5} = 1.2 \times 10^5$ J

$W = 120$ kJ

Answer: $120$

questions.q: A thermodynamic system is taken through the cyclic process $A B C$ as shown in the figure. The total work done by the system during the cycle $A B C$ is $\_\_\_\_$ J.
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
questions.solution:
From the P-V diagram: A(2,100), B(5,300), C(5,100) in Pa and m³ units.
Process A→B is linear. Equation: $P = 100 + \frac{200}{3}(V-2)$
$W_{AB} = \int_2^5 \frac{200V - 100}{3} dV = \frac{1}{3}[100V^2 - 100V]_2^5 = \frac{1800}{3} = 600$ J
Process B→C is isobaric: $W_{BC} = 300(5-5) = 0$ J
Process C→A is isobaric: $W_{CA} = 100(2-5) = -300$ J
Total work done by system: $W = 600 + 0 - 300 = 300$ J

questions.q: In the following $p-V$ diagram the equation of state along the curved path is given by $(V-2)^{2}=4 a p$ where $a$ is a constant. The total work done in the closed path is
questions.solution:
From the equation of state $(V-2)^2 = 4ap$, we get $p = \frac{(V-2)^2}{4a}$.
At V = 1: $p = \frac{1}{4a}$ and at V = 3: $p = \frac{1}{4a}$.
The curved path A→B→C follows the given equation, while C→A is a straight line at constant pressure.
Work along the curved path:
$W_{ABC} = \int_1^3 \frac{(V-2)^2}{4a} dV = \frac{1}{4a}\left[\frac{(V-2)^3}{3}\right]_1^3 = \frac{1}{4a} \cdot \frac{2}{3} = \frac{1}{6a}$.
Work along C→A at constant pressure:
$W_{CA} = \frac{1}{4a}(1-3) = -\frac{1}{2a}$.
Total work: $W_{total} = \frac{1}{6a} - \frac{1}{2a} = -\frac{1}{3a}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: 10 mole of an ideal gas is undergoing the process shown in the figure. The heat involved in the process from $P_{1} to P_{2}$ is $\alpha$ Joule ($P_{1}=21.7 \mathrm{~Pa}$ and $\left.P_{2}=30 \mathrm{~Pa}, \mathrm{C}_{v}=21 \mathrm{~J} / \mathrm{K}. \mathrm{mol}, R=8.3 \mathrm{~J} / \mathrm{mol}. \mathrm{K}\right)$. The value of $\alpha$ is $\_\_\_\_$.
questions.solution:
From the given $P-V$ diagram, the process from $P_1$ to $P_2$ is an isochoric process because the volume remains constant at $V = 1\text{ m}^3$.
For an isochoric process, the work done $W = 0$.
According to the first law of thermodynamics, the heat involved is $Q = \Delta U + W = \Delta U$.
The change in internal energy is given by $\Delta U = n C_v \Delta T$.
Using the ideal gas equation $PV = nRT$, we have $n\Delta T = \frac{V\Delta P}{R}$.
Substituting this into the expression for $Q$:
$Q = C_v \left( \frac{V(P_2 - P_1)}{R} \right)$
Given values: $n = 10$ moles, $V = 1\text{ m}^3$, $P_1 = 21.7\text{ Pa}$, $P_2 = 30\text{ Pa}$, $C_v = 21\text{ J/mol}\cdot\text{K}$, and $R = 8.3\text{ J/mol}\cdot\text{K}$.
$Q = 21 \times \frac{1 \times (30 - 21.7)}{8.3}$
$Q = 21 \times \frac{8.3}{8.3} = 21\text{ J}$.
Thus, the value of $\alpha$ is 21.

Density of water at $4{ }^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ and $20^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ are $1000 \mathrm{~kg} / \mathrm{m}^{3}$ and $998 \mathrm{~kg} / \mathrm{m}^{3}$ respectively. The increase in internal energy of 4 kg of water when it is heated from $4{ }^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ to $20^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ is $\_\_\_\_$ J.
(specific heat capacity of water $=4.2 \mathrm{~J} / \mathrm{kg}$. and 1 atmospheric pressure $=10^{5} \mathrm{~Pa}$)
questions.solution:
Heat absorbed by water: $Q = mc\Delta T = 4 \times 4200 \times 16 = 268800$ J.
Volume change: $V_1 = 4/1000 = 0.004$ m³ at 4°C, $V_2 = 4/998 ≈ 0.00401$ m³ at 20°C.
Work done by water at constant pressure: $W = P_{atm}\Delta V = 10^5 \times 0.00001 = 0.8$ J.
By first law of thermodynamics: $\Delta U = Q - W = 268800 - 0.8 = 268799.2$ J

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
One mole of an ideal diatomic gas expands from volume $V$ to 2 V isothermally at a temperature $27^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ and does $W$ joule of work. If the gas undergoes same magnitude of expansion adiabatically from $27^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ doing the same amount of work $W$, then its final temperature will be (close to) $\_\_\_\_ { }^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$.
$\left(\log _{\mathrm{e}} 2=0.693\right)$
questions.solution:
For isothermal expansion of 1 mole diatomic gas from V to 2V at 300 K:
$W = RT\ln 2 = R(300)\ln 2$
For adiabatic expansion with same volume change and same work output:
$W = nC_V\Delta T = C_V(T_i - T_f)$
For diatomic gas, $C_V = \frac{5}{2}R$. Setting work equal:
$R(300)\ln 2 = \frac{5}{2}R(300 - T_f)$
Simplifying:
$300\ln 2 = 2.5(300 - T_f)$, so $300(0.693) = 2.5(300 - T_f)$
$207.9 = 750 - 2.5T_f$, giving $T_f = 216.84$ K $\approx$ -56°C.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
The internal energy of a monoatomic gas is 3 nRT. One mole of helium is kept in a cylinder having internal cross section area of $17 \mathrm{~cm}^{2}$ and fitted with a light movable frictionless piston. The gas is heated slowly by suppling 126 J heat. If the temperature rises by $4^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$, then the piston will move $\_\_\_\_$ cm.
(atmospheric pressure $=10^{5} \mathrm{~Pa}$)
questions.solution:
The question states the internal energy of the gas is $U = 3nRT$.
The change in internal energy is $\Delta U = 3nR\Delta T$.
Given: $n = 1$ mole, $\Delta T = 4^{\circ}C = 4$ K, and $R \approx 8.314$ J/mol·K.
$\Delta U = 3 \times 1 \times 8.314 \times 4 = 99.768$ J.
According to the first law of thermodynamics, $\Delta Q = \Delta U + W$.
Given heat supplied $\Delta Q = 126$ J.
Work done by the gas $W = \Delta Q - \Delta U = 126 - 99.768 = 26.232$ J.
Since the piston is light and movable, the process occurs at constant atmospheric pressure $P = 10^5$ Pa.
Work done $W = P \Delta V = P(A \times d)$, where $A$ is the cross-section area and $d$ is the displacement of the piston.
$A = 17 \text{ cm}^2 = 17 \times 10^{-4} \text{ m}^2$.
$26.232 = 10^5 \times (17 \times 10^{-4}) \times d$.
$26.232 = 170 \times d$.
$d = \frac{26.232}{170} \approx 0.1543$ m.
Converting to cm: $d \approx 15.43$ cm.
Rounding to the nearest option, we get $15.5$ cm.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A diatomic gas $(\gamma=1.4)$ does 100 J of work when it is expanded isobarically. Then the heat given to the gas $\_\_\_\_$ J.
questions.solution:
For an isobaric process, the first law gives: $Q = \Delta U + W$.
For a diatomic gas with $\gamma = 1.4$, we have $C_V = \frac{5}{2}R$ and $C_P = \frac{7}{2}R$.
Since $W = nR\Delta T = 100$ J for isobaric expansion, the change in internal energy is: $\Delta U = nC_V\Delta T = \frac{5}{2}nR\Delta T = \frac{5}{2} \times 100 = 250$ J.
Therefore, $Q = 250 + 100 = 350$ J.

questions.q: There are two vessels filled with an ideal gas where volume of one is double the volume of other. The large vessel contains the gas at 8 kPa at 1000 K while the smaller vessel contains the gas at 7 kPa at 500 K. If the vessels are connected to each other by a thin tube allowing the gas to flow and the temperature of both vessels is maintained at 600 K , at steady state the pressure in the vessels will be (in kPa).
questions.solution:
Number of masses will remain constant
$\begin{aligned}
& \mathrm{n}_1+\mathrm{n}_2=\mathrm{n}_{\mathrm{f}} \\ & \frac{\mathrm{P}_1 \mathrm{~V}_1}{\mathrm{RT}_1}+\frac{\mathrm{P}_2 \mathrm{~V}_2}{\mathrm{RT}_2}=\frac{\mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{f}} \mathrm{~V}_{\mathrm{f}}}{\mathrm{RT}_{\mathrm{f}}} \\ & \frac{8 \times 2 \mathrm{~V}}{\mathrm{R} \times 1000}+\frac{7 \times \mathrm{V}}{\mathrm{R} \times 500}=\frac{\mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{f}}(3 \mathrm{~V})}{\mathrm{R} \times 600} \\ & \frac{16}{1000}+\frac{14}{1000}=\frac{\mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{f}}}{\mathrm{R} \times 600} \\ & \frac{30}{1000}=\frac{\mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{f}}}{200} \\ & \mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{f}}=6 \mathrm{kPa}
\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: During the melting of a slab of ice at 273 K at atmospheric pressure :
options: Internal energy of ice-water system remains unchanged.
Positive work is done by the ice-water system on the atmosphere.
Internal energy of the ice-water system decreases.
Positive work is done on the ice-water system by the atmosphere.
questions.solution:
Volume decreases during melting of ice so positive work is done on ice water system by atmosphere
Heat absorbed by ice water so $\Delta $\mathrm{Q}$ is positive, work done by ice water system is negative
Hence by first law of thermodynamics
$\Delta $\mathrm{U}=$\Delta $\mathrm{Q}+$\Delta $\mathrm{W}=$\text{ Positive }$
So internal energy increases

(Take $\gamma=1.5: \gamma$ is the ratio of specific heats at constant pressure and at constant volume)
questions.solution:
$\begin{aligned}& \mathrm{V}_1=800 \mathrm{ cm}^3 \quad \mathrm{ V}_2=200 \mathrm{ cm}^3 \\
& \mathrm{ T}_1=300 \mathrm{ K}\end{aligned}$for adiabatic$\begin{aligned}& \mathrm{TV}^{\gamma-1}=\text{ const. } \\

& \mathrm{ T}_2=600 \mathrm{ K} \\
& \Delta \mathrm{ T}=600-300=300 \mathrm{ K}\end{aligned}$

questions.q:
A Carnot engine $(\mathrm{E})$ is working between two temperatures 473 K and 273 K . In a new system two engines - engine $E_1$ works between 473 K to 373 K and engine $E_2$ works between 373 K to 273 K .
If $\eta_{12}, \eta_1$ and $\eta_2$ are the efficiencies of the engines $E, E_1$ and $E_2$, respectively, then
questions.solution:
Efficiencies of a carnot engine $\eta=1-\frac{T_{\text{sink }}}{T_{\text{source }}} \begin{aligned}
\Rightarrow & \eta_1=1-\frac{373 \mathrm{ K}}{473 \mathrm{ K}}=\frac{100}{473} \\
& \eta_2=1-\frac{273 \mathrm{ K}}{373 \mathrm{ K}}=\frac{100}{373} \\
& \eta_{12}=1-\frac{273 \mathrm{ K}}{473 \mathrm{ K}}=\frac{100}{473} \\
& \eta_{12}-\eta_1=\frac{200}{473}-\frac{100}{473}=\frac{100}{473} < \frac{100}{373} \\
\Rightarrow & \eta_{12}-\eta_1 < \eta_2 \\
\text{$ or $} & \eta_{12} < \eta_1+\eta_2
\end{aligned}$

questions.q:
Given below are two statements. One is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).
Assertion (A) : In an insulated container, a gas is adiabatically shrunk to half of its initial volume. The temperature of the gas decreases.
Reason (R): Free expansion of an ideal gas is an irreversible and an adiabatic process.
In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below :
options: Both $(\mathbf{A})$ and $(\mathbf{R})$ are true but $(\mathbf{R})$ is NOT the correct explanation of $(\mathbf{A})$
Both $(\mathbf{A})$ and $(\mathbf{R})$ are true and $(\mathbf{R})$ is the correct explanation of $(\mathbf{A})$
questions.solution:
If the container is insulated then temperature is expected to increase in adiabatic compression. So (A) is wrong.
And free expansion is irreversible and adiabatic process. So (R) is correct.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
An ideal gas goes from an initial state to final state. During the process, the pressure of gas increases linearly with temperature.
A. The work done by gas during the process is zero.
B. The heat added to gas is different from change in its internal energy.
C. The volume of the gas is increased.
D. The internal energy of the gas is increased.
E. The process is isochoric (constant volume process)
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.solution:
Given that
$\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{kT} \frac{\mathrm{P}}{\mathrm{ T}}=\text{ constant }$ \therefore$ Volume is constant or isochoric process.
$\begin{aligned}
& \therefore $\mathrm{W}_{\mathrm{D}$}=0 \\
& \therefore $\mathrm{Q}=$\Delta $\mathrm{U}$
\end{aligned}$

Also temperature increases hence internal energy increases.$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The temperature of 1 mole of an ideal monoatomic gas is increased by $50^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ at constant pressure. The total heat added and change in internal energy are $E_1$ and $E_2$, respectively. If $\frac{E_1}{E_2}=\frac{x}{9}$ then the value of $x$ is _____
questions.solution:
Given that process is isobaric $\Delta \mathrm{T}=50^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$
Q in isobaric process $=\mathrm{nC}_{\mathrm{p}} \Delta \mathrm{T}=\mathrm{E}_1 \Delta \mathrm{U}$ in isobaric process $=\mathrm{nC}_{\mathrm{v}} \Delta \mathrm{T}=\mathrm{E}_2 \therefore \frac{\mathrm{E}_1}{\mathrm{E}_2}=\frac{\mathrm{C}_{\mathrm{P}}}{\mathrm{C}_{\mathrm{v}}}=\gamma$

Given, gas is monoatomic
$\begin{aligned}
\therefore \gamma & =1+\frac{2}{\mathrm{f}} \\
& =1+\frac{2}{3} \\
& =\frac{5}{3}
\end{aligned}$

Now, as per question.
$\begin{aligned}
& \frac{5}{3}=\frac{x}{9} \\
& x=15
\end{aligned}$

questions.q: Water of mass $m$ gram is slowly heated to increase the temperature from $T_1$ to $T_z$ The change in entropy of the water, given specific heat of water is $1 \mathrm{Jkg}^{-1} \mathrm{~K}^{-1}$, is :
questions.solution: $\begin{aligned} & d \mathrm{Q}=\mathrm{msdT} \\ & \mathrm{dS}=\frac{\mathrm{dQ}}{\mathrm{T}}=\frac{\mathrm{msdT}}{\mathrm{T}} \\ & \Delta \mathrm{S}=\int \frac{\mathrm{msdT}}{\mathrm{T}}=\mathrm{ms} \ln \frac{\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{f}}}{\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{i}}} \\ & \Delta \mathrm{S}=\mathrm{m} \ln \frac{\mathrm{T}_2}{\mathrm{~T}_1}\end{aligned}$

questions.solution: $\begin{aligned} & \gamma=\frac{3}{2} \\ & \mathrm{Tv}^{\gamma-1}=\mathrm{C} \\ & 273 \mathrm{~V}_0^{0.5}=\mathrm{T}\left(\frac{\mathrm{V}_0}{4}\right)^{0.5} \\ & \mathrm{~T}=273 \times 2=546 \\ & \Delta \mathrm{~T}=273\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A sample of 1 mole gas at temperature $\mathrm{T}$ is adiabatically expanded to double its volume. If adiabatic constant for the gas is $\gamma=\frac{3}{2}$, then the work done by the gas in the process is:
questions.solution: $\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{TV}^{\gamma-1}=\text{ constant } \\ & \Rightarrow \mathrm{T}(\mathrm{V})^{\frac{3}{2}-1}=\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{f}}(2 \mathrm{ V})^{\frac{3}{2}-1} \\ & \Rightarrow \mathrm{TV}^{\frac{1}{2}}=\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{f}}(2)^{\frac{1}{2}}(\mathrm{ V})^{\frac{1}{2}} \\ & \Rightarrow \mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{f}}=\left(\frac{\mathrm{T}}{\sqrt{2}}\right) \\ & \text{ Now, W.D. }=\frac{\mathrm{nR} \Delta \mathrm{T}}{1-\gamma}=\frac{1 \cdot \mathrm{R}\left[\frac{\mathrm{T}}{\sqrt{2}}-\mathrm{T}\right]}{1-\frac{3}{2}} \\ & \Rightarrow \text{ W.D. }=2 \mathrm{RT}\left[1-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right] \\ & \Rightarrow \text{ W.D. }=\mathrm{RT}[2-\sqrt{2}]\end{aligned}$
questions.question: A sample of 1 mole gas at temperature $\mathrm{T}$ is adiabatically expanded to double its volume. If adiabatic constant for the gas is $\gamma=\frac{3}{2}$, then the work done by the gas in the process is:
questions.explanation: $\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{TV}^{\gamma-1}=\text{ constant } \\ & \Rightarrow \mathrm{T}(\mathrm{V})^{\frac{3}{2}-1}=\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{f}}(2 \mathrm{ V})^{\frac{3}{2}-1} \\ & \Rightarrow \mathrm{TV}^{\frac{1}{2}}=\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{f}}(2)^{\frac{1}{2}}(\mathrm{ V})^{\frac{1}{2}} \\ & \Rightarrow \mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{f}}=\left(\frac{\mathrm{T}}{\sqrt{2}}\right) \\ & \text{ Now, W.D. }=\frac{\mathrm{nR} \Delta \mathrm{T}}{1-\gamma}=\frac{1 \cdot \mathrm{R}\left[\frac{\mathrm{T}}{\sqrt{2}}-\mathrm{T}\right]}{1-\frac{3}{2}} \\ & \Rightarrow \text{ W.D. }=2 \mathrm{RT}\left[1-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right] \\ & \Rightarrow \text{ W.D. }=\mathrm{RT}[2-\sqrt{2}]\end{aligned}$

questions.q: The volume of an ideal gas $(\gamma=1.5)$ is changed adiabatically from 5 litres to 4 litres. The ratio of initial pressure to final pressure is:
questions.solution:
For Adiabatic process
$\begin{aligned} & P_i V_i=P_f V_f^\gamma \\ & P_i(5)^{1.5}=P_f(4)^{1.5} \\ & \frac{P_i}{P_f}=\left(\frac{4}{5}\right)^{\frac{3}{2}}=\frac{4}{5} \cdot\left(\frac{4}{5}\right)^{\frac{1}{2}} \Rightarrow \frac{8}{5 \sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A diatomic gas $(\gamma=1.4)$ does $100 \mathrm{~J}$ of work in an isobaric expansion. The heat given to the gas is :
questions.solution:
For Isobaric process $\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{w}=\mathrm{P} \Delta \mathrm{v}=\mathrm{nR} \Delta \mathrm{T}=100 \mathrm{~J} \\ & \mathrm{Q}=\Delta \mathrm{u}+\mathrm{w} \\ & \Delta \mathrm{Q}=\frac{\mathrm{F}}{2} \mathrm{nR} \Delta \mathrm{T}+\mathrm{nR} \Delta \mathrm{T} \\ & \left(\frac{\mathrm{f}}{2}+1\right) \mathrm{nR} \Delta \mathrm{T} \\ & \left(\frac{5}{2}+1\right) 100=350 \mathrm{~J}\end{aligned}$
SECTION - B

questions.q: Two different adiabatic paths for the same gas intersect two isothermal curves as shown in P-V diagram. The relation between the ratio $\frac{V_a}{V_d}$ and the ratio $\frac{V_b}{V_c}$ is:
questions.solution:
For adiabatic process
$\mathrm{TV}^{\gamma-1}=$ constant
$\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{a}} \cdot \mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{a}}^{\gamma-1}=\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{d}} \cdot \mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{d}}^{\gamma-1} \\ & \left(\frac{\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{a}}}{\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{d}}}\right)^{\gamma-1}=\frac{\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{d}}}{\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{a}}} \\ & \mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{b}} \cdot \mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{b}}^{\gamma-1}=\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{c}} \cdot \mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{c}}^{\gamma-1} \\ & \left(\frac{\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{b}}}{\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{c}}}\right)^{\gamma-1}=\frac{\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{c}}}{\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{b}}} \\ & \frac{\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{a}}}{\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{d}}}=\frac{\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{b}}}{\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{c}}} \quad\left($\begin{array}{c}\because $\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{d}$}=$\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{c}$} \\ $\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{a}$}=$\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{b}$}\end{array}$\right)\end{aligned}$
questions.question: Two different adiabatic paths for the same gas intersect two isothermal curves as shown in P-V diagram. The relation between the ratio $\frac{V_a}{V_d}$ and the ratio $\frac{V_b}{V_c}$ is:
questions.explanation:
For adiabatic process
$\mathrm{TV}^{\gamma-1}=$ constant
$\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{a}} \cdot \mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{a}}^{\gamma-1}=\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{d}} \cdot \mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{d}}^{\gamma-1} \\ & \left(\frac{\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{a}}}{\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{d}}}\right)^{\gamma-1}=\frac{\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{d}}}{\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{a}}} \\ & \mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{b}} \cdot \mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{b}}^{\gamma-1}=\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{c}} \cdot \mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{c}}^{\gamma-1} \\ & \left(\frac{\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{b}}}{\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{c}}}\right)^{\gamma-1}=\frac{\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{c}}}{\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{b}}} \\ & \frac{\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{a}}}{\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{d}}}=\frac{\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{b}}}{\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{c}}} \quad\left($\begin{array}{c}\because $\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{d}$}=$\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{c}$} \\ $\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{a}$}=$\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{b}$}\end{array}$\right)\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
A total of $48 \mathrm{~J}$ heat is given to one mole of helium kept in a cylinder. The temperature of helium increases by $2^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$. The work done by the gas is:
Given, $\mathrm{R}=8.3 \mathrm{~J} \mathrm{~K}^{-1} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$.
questions.solution:
$1^{\text{st }}$ law of thermodynamics
$\begin{aligned}
& \Delta \mathrm{Q}=\Delta \mathrm{U}+\mathrm{W} \\
& \Rightarrow+48=\mathrm{nC}_{\mathrm{v}} \Delta \mathrm{T}+\mathrm{W} \\
& \Rightarrow 48=(1)\left(\frac{3 \mathrm{R}}{2}\right)(2)+\mathrm{W} \\
& \Rightarrow \mathrm{W}=48-3 \times \mathrm{R} \\
& \Rightarrow \mathrm{W}=48-3 \times(8.3) \\
& \Rightarrow \mathrm{W}=23.1 \text{ Joule }
\end{aligned}$

A sample of gas at temperature $T$ is adiabatically expanded to double its volume. Adiabatic constant for the gas is $\gamma=3 / 2$. The work done by the gas in the process is:
$(\mu=1 \mathrm{~mole})$

questions.q: A diatomic gas $( \gamma = 1 . 4 )$ does $200J$ of work when it is expanded isobarically. The heat given to the gas in the process is :
questions.solution:
For degree of freedom, we can write

$\gamma = 1 + \dfrac{2}{f} = 1 . 4 ⇒ \dfrac{2}{f} = 0 . 4$

$⇒ f = 5$

For isobaric process, $W = nR\DeltaT = 200J$.

Now, we can write

$Q = \left(\dfrac{f + 2}{2}\right)nR \Delta T$

$= \dfrac{7}{2} \times 200 = 700J$

$∴ W = \dfrac{{P}_{2}{V}_{2} - {P}_{1}{V}_{1}}{- \dfrac{1}{2}}$

questions.q: A thermodynamic system is taken from an original state $A$ to an intermediate state $B$ by a linear process as shown in the figure. Its volume is then reduced to the original value from $B$ to $C$ by an isobaric process. The total work done by the gas from $A$ to $B$ and $B$ to $C$ would be :
questions.solution:
Work done during the path $A \to B$ can be written as $\begin{cases}{W}_{AB} & = & \dfrac{1}{2} ( 8000 + 4000 ) dyne{cm}^{- 2} \times \dfrac{1N}{{10}^{5}dyne} \times \dfrac{1{cm}^{2}}{{10}^{- 4}{m}^{2}} \times \left(7 - 3\right){m}^{3} \\ & = & 2400J\end{cases}$

The work done during the process $B \to C$ is given by

$\begin{cases}{W}_{BC} & = & \left(4000dyne{cm}^{- 2} \times \dfrac{1N}{{10}^{5}dyne} \times \dfrac{1{cm}^{2}}{{10}^{- 4}{m}^{2}}\right) \times \left(3 - 7\right){m}^{3} \\ & = & - 1600J\end{cases}$

Hence, the total work done is given by

$\begin{cases}W & = & {W}_{AB} + {W}_{BC} \\ & = & 2400J - 1600J \\ & = & 800J\end{cases}$

questions.q: During an adiabatic process, the pressure of a gas is found to be proportional to the cube of its absolute temperature. The ratio of $\dfrac{{C}_{p}}{{C}_{v}}$ for the gas is :
questions.solution:
It is given that

$P ∝ {T}^{3} ⇒ P{T}^{- 3} = \text{constant} . . . \left(1\right)$

For an adiabatic process,

$P{V}^{\gamma} = \text{constant} . . . \left(2\right)$

Assuming the gas to be a perfect gas, it can be written from equation (2) that

$P{\left(\dfrac{nRT}{P}\right)}^{\gamma} = \text{constant} ⇒ {P}^{1 - \gamma}{T}^{\gamma} = \text{constant} ⇒ PT\dfrac{\gamma}{1 - \gamma} = \text{constant}$

By comparing with equation(1), we get

$⇒ \dfrac{\gamma}{1 - \gamma} = - 3 ⇒ \gamma = - 3 + 3\gamma ⇒ 3 = 2\gamma ⇒ \gamma = \dfrac{3}{2}$

By comparing with equation(1), we get

$⇒ \dfrac{\gamma}{1 - \gamma} = - 3 ⇒ \gamma = - 3 + 3\gamma ⇒ 3 = 2\gamma ⇒ \gamma = \dfrac{3}{2}$

The amount of work done for the given process should be zero, as the process is an isochoric process.

$Q = ∆ U$

$∆ U = ms ∆ T . . . \left(1\right)$

From equation (1), it follows that

$\begin{cases}∆ U & = & 0 . 08 \times ( 170 \times 4 . 18 ) \times 5J \\ & \approx & 284J\end{cases}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A gas is compressed adiabatically, which one of the following statement is NOT true?
options: There is no heat supplied to the system
There is no change in the internal energy
The change in the internal energy is equal to the work done on the gas
questions.solution:
In adiabatic process,

$∆ Q = 0$ and $∆ U \ne 0$

Using the first law of thermodynamics, $∆ Q = ∆ U + W$

$⇒ ∆ U = - W\left(W\text{is the work done by the gas}, \text{so} - W\text{will be the work done on the gas}\right)$

As the gas is compressed

$W < 0$

Therefore, $∆ U > 0$ and hence $∆ T > 0$.

questions.q: Consider two containers $A and B$ containing monoatomic gases at the same Pressure $\left(P\right)$, Volume $\left(V\right)$ and Temperature $\left(T\right)$. The gas in $A$ is compressed isothermally to $\dfrac{1}{8}$ of its original volume while the gas in $B$ is compressed adiabatically to $\dfrac{1}{8}$ of its original volume. The ratio of final pressure of gas in $B$ to that of gas in $A$ is
questions.solution:
In an isothermal process the temperature is constant.

$PV = nRT$

So, it can be written that

$PV = {P}_{A}\left(\dfrac{V}{8}\right) ⇒ {P}_{A} = 8P$

In an adiabatic process,

$P{V}^{\gamma} =$constant

$\gamma$ for monoatomic gas is $\dfrac{5}{3}$

So, it can be written

$\dfrac{{P}_{B}}{P} = \left(\dfrac{V}{\dfrac{V}{8}}\right)\dfrac{5}{3} ⇒ {P}_{B} = 32P$

Thus, the ratio of the pressures is

$\dfrac{{P}_{B}}{{P}_{A}} = \dfrac{32P}{8P} = 4$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Work done by a Carnot engine operating between temperatures $127 ° C$ and $27 ° C$ is $2kJ$. The amount of heat transferred to the engine by the reservoir is:
questions.solution:
The temperatures in Kelvin scales are

${T}_{2} = 27 ° C + 273 = 300K{T}_{1} = 127 ° C + 273 = 400K$

The efficiency of the Carnot engine is

$η = 1 - \dfrac{{T}_{2}}{{T}_{1}} = 1 - \dfrac{300}{400} = \dfrac{1}{4}$
Using the relation, $η = \dfrac{W}{Q}$
$⇒ \dfrac{2kJ}{Q} = \dfrac{1}{4} ⇒ Q = 8kJ$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: If heat is added to a system, its temperature must increase.

Statement II: If positive work is done by a system in a thermodynamic process, its volume must increase.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below
options: Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
questions.solution:
If heat energy is added to a thermodynamic system, one part increases the internal energy and the other part performs some work.

If heat is added to a system, the system can do work without changing its internal energy. Hence, statement 1 is false.

The formula to calculate the work done is given by

$W = ∫ PdV$

From the above equation, it can be concluded that if $W > 0$, i.e., work is done by the system, its volume must increase. Hence, statement II is true.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A source supplies heat to a system at the rate of $1000W .$ If the system performs work at a rate of $200W .$ The rate at which internal energy of the system increases is
questions.solution:
According to the first law of thermodynamics, $Q = W + U$.

Upon differentiation, we get

$\dfrac{dQ}{dt} = \dfrac{dW}{dt} + \dfrac{dU}{dt} ⇒ \dfrac{dU}{dt} = \dfrac{dQ}{dt} - \dfrac{dW}{dt}$

Given: $\dfrac{dQ}{dt} = 1000W$

$\dfrac{dW}{dt} = 200W$

Therefore, $\dfrac{dU}{dt} = 1000W - 200W = 800W$

Given: $\dfrac{dQ}{dt} = 1000W$

$\dfrac{dW}{dt} = 200W$

Therefore, $\dfrac{dU}{dt} = 1000W - 200W = 800W$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A Carnot engine operating between two reservoirs has efficiency $\dfrac{1}{3}$. When the temperature of cold reservoir raised by $x$, its efficiency decreases to $\dfrac{1}{6}$. The value of $x$, if the temperature of hot reservoir is $99 ° C$, will be
questions.solution:
A carnot engine works between two reservoirs, one hot reservoir and one cold reservoir.

The absolute temperature $\left({T}_{H}\right)$ of the hot reservoir can be calculated as follows-

$\begin{cases}{T}_{H} & = & 99 ° C \\ & = & 99 + 273K \\ & = & 372K\end{cases}$

The formula to calculate the efficiency $\left(η\right)$ of the engine is given by

$η = 1 - \dfrac{{T}_{C}}{{T}_{H}} . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . ( 1 )$

where, ${T}_{C}$ is the temperature of the cold reservoir.

Substituting the values of the known parameters in equation (1), we get

$\begin{cases}\dfrac{1}{3} & = & 1 - \dfrac{{T}_{C}}{{T}_{H}} \\ & ⇒ & \dfrac{{T}_{C}}{{T}_{H}} = \dfrac{2}{3} \\ & ⇒ & {T}_{C} = \dfrac{2}{3} \times 372K \\ & = & 248K\end{cases}$

The new efficiency of the engine $\left(η '\right)$ is given by

$η ' = 1 - \dfrac{{T}_{C} + X}{{T}_{H}} . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . ( 2 )$

Substituting $\dfrac{1}{6}$ for $η '$ and the known values of the temperatures into equation (2), we get

$\begin{cases}\dfrac{1}{6} & = & 1 - \dfrac{{T}_{C} + X}{{T}_{H}} \\ ⇒ & \dfrac{5}{6} = \dfrac{{T}_{C} + X}{{T}_{H}} \\ ⇒ & 248 + X = 5 \times 62 \\ ⇒ & X = 310 - 248 \\ = & 62K\end{cases}$

A carnot engine works between two reservoirs, one hot reservoir and one cold reservoir.

The absolute temperature $\left({T}_{H}\right)$ of the hot reservoir can be calculated as follows-

where, ${T}_{C}$ is the temperature of the cold reservoir.

Substituting the values of the known parameters in equation (1), we get

$\begin{cases}\dfrac{1}{3} & = & 1 - \dfrac{{T}_{C}}{{T}_{H}} \\ & ⇒ & \dfrac{{T}_{C}}{{T}_{H}} = \dfrac{2}{3} \\ & ⇒ & {T}_{C} = \dfrac{2}{3} \times 372K \\ & = & 248K\end{cases}$

The new efficiency of the engine $\left(η '\right)$ is given by

$η ' = 1 - \dfrac{{T}_{C} + X}{{T}_{H}} . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . ( 2 )$

Substituting $\dfrac{1}{6}$ for $η '$ and the known values of the temperatures into equation (2), we get

$\begin{cases}\dfrac{1}{6} & = & 1 - \dfrac{{T}_{C} + X}{{T}_{H}} \\ ⇒ & \dfrac{5}{6} = \dfrac{{T}_{C} + X}{{T}_{H}} \\ ⇒ & 248 + X = 5 \times 62 \\ ⇒ & X = 310 - 248 \\ = & 62K\end{cases}$

questions.q: A sample of gas at temperature $T$ is adiabatically expanded to double its volume. The work done by the gas in the process is given, (given $\gamma = \dfrac{3}{2}$) :
questions.solution:
Work done by gas in adiabatic process is:

$W = - \dfrac{\left({P}_{2}{V}_{2} - {P}_{1}{V}_{1}\right)}{\gamma - 1}$

$= - \dfrac{nR\left({T}_{2} - {T}_{1}\right)}{\gamma - 1}$

For an adiabatic process, ${T}_{1}{{V}_{1}}^{\gamma - 1} = {T}_{2}{{V}_{2}}^{\gamma - 1}$

$⇒ T{V}^{\dfrac{3}{2} - 1} = {T}_{2}{\left(2V\right)}^{\dfrac{3}{2} - 1} ⇒ TV\dfrac{1}{2} = {T}_{2}\left(2V\right)\dfrac{1}{2} ⇒ {T}_{2} = \dfrac{T}{\sqrt{2}}$

Now, work done is $W = \dfrac{R\left({T}_{1} - {T}_{2}\right)}{\gamma - 1} = \dfrac{R\left(T - \dfrac{T}{\sqrt{2}}\right)}{\dfrac{1}{2}} = RT\left(2 - \sqrt{2}\right)$

$= - \dfrac{nR\left({T}_{2} - {T}_{1}\right)}{\gamma - 1}$

For an adiabatic process, ${T}_{1}{{V}_{1}}^{\gamma - 1} = {T}_{2}{{V}_{2}}^{\gamma - 1}$

$⇒ T{V}^{\dfrac{3}{2} - 1} = {T}_{2}{\left(2V\right)}^{\dfrac{3}{2} - 1} ⇒ TV\dfrac{1}{2} = {T}_{2}\left(2V\right)\dfrac{1}{2} ⇒ {T}_{2} = \dfrac{T}{\sqrt{2}}$

Now, work done is $W = \dfrac{R\left({T}_{1} - {T}_{2}\right)}{\gamma - 1} = \dfrac{R\left(T - \dfrac{T}{\sqrt{2}}\right)}{\dfrac{1}{2}} = RT\left(2 - \sqrt{2}\right)$

questions.q: Heat energy of $735J$ is given to a diatomic gas allowing the gas to expand at constant pressure. Each gas molecule rotates around an internal axis but do not oscillate. The increase in the internal energy of the gas will be:

For isobaric process and diatomic gas we can write, $\DeltaQ = n{C}_{P}\DeltaT = 735J$

$= 525J$

Given below are two statements : one is labelled as Assertion A and the other is labelled as Reason R.

Assertion A : Efficiency of a reversible heat engine will be highest at $– 273 ° C$ temperature of cold reservoir.

Reason R : The efficiency of Carnot’s engine depends not only on temperature of cold reservoir but it depends on the temperature of hot reservoir too and is given as $η = \left(1 - \dfrac{{T}_{2}}{{T}_{1}}\right)$

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below :
options: A is true but R is false
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
questions.solution:

Therefore, both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
Heat is given to an ideal gas in an isothermal process.

A. Internal energy of the gas will decrease.

B. Internal energy of the gas will increase.

C. Internal energy of the gas will not change.

D. The gas will do positive work.

E. The gas will do negative work.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below :
questions.solution:
From the first law of thermodynamics, heat supplied to the system $Q$, change in internal energy of the system $∆ U$ and work done by the system $W$ are related as:

$Q = ∆ U + W$

Since the process is isothermal, the temperature of the system is constant and therefore $∆ U = 0$ (i.e., internal energy is constant).

$⇒ Q = W$

As heat is supplied to the system, $Q$ is positive and therefore $W$ is positive i.e., gas will do positive work.

Hence, correct options are C and D.

questions.q:
Given below are two statements. One is labelled as Assertion A and the other is labelled as Reason R.

Assertion A : If $dQ$ and $dW$ represent the heat supplied to the system and the work done on the system respectively. Then according to the first law of thermodynamics $dQ = dU - dW$.

Reason R : First law of thermodynamics is based on law of conservation of energy.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the option given below :
options: A is correct but R is not correct
A is not correct but R is correct
Both A and R are correct and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are correct but R is not the correct explanation of A
questions.solution:
The first law of thermodynamics is stated as $dQ = dU - dW$. Since $dQ$ is heat supplied to the system and positive thus, $dW$ is work done on the system, i.e., negative work.

We know that the first law of thermodynamics deals with work done, and heat energy supplied or removed from a system. Therefore, it is based on the conservation of energy. The law states that energy cannot be created or destroyed; it can only be converted from one form to another.

questions.solution:

Match List I with List II :

List I List II
A Isothermal Process I Work done by the gas decreases internal energy
B Adiabatic Process II No change in internal energy
C Isochoric Process III The heat absorbed goes partly to increase internal energy and partly to do work
D Isobaric Process IV No work is done on or by the gas

Choose the correct answer from the options given below :
questions.solution:
(A) Change in internal energy is expressed as$∆ U = n{C}_{v} ∆ T$, here, $∆ T$ is change in temperature.

Since, in an isothermal process temperature remains constant, thus, $∆ U = 0$

$A \to II$

(B) In an adiabatic process, heat transfer, $Q = 0$.

So, from first law of thermodynamics,

$Q = ∆ U + W$

$∆ U = - W$

Since, work done by gas is positive, thus, $∆ U$ is negative

$B \to I$

(C) In an isochoric process, volume remains constant, so work done by or on the gas $W = P ∆ V = 0$

$C \to IV$

(D) In an isobaric process, pressure remains constant, so work done$W = P ∆ V \ne 0$ and change in internal energy $∆ U = n{C}_{v} ∆ T \ne 0$

Thus, heat absorbed goes partly to increase internal energy and partly do work.

$D \to III$

questions.q: A Carnot engine with efficiency $50 %$ takes heat from a source at $600K$. In order to increase the efficiency to $70 %$, keeping the temperature of sink same, the new temperature of the source will be:
questions.solution:
Efficiency of Carnot engine is given by $η = 1 - \dfrac{{T}_{sink}}{{T}_{source}} = 1 - \dfrac{{T}_{2}}{{T}_{1}}$

Given: Initial efficiency $η = \dfrac{1}{2}$

$∴ \dfrac{1}{2} = 1 - \dfrac{{T}_{2}}{600}$

$⇒ \dfrac{{T}_{2}}{600} = \dfrac{1}{2}$

$⇒ {T}_{2} = 300K$

When efficiency is increased to $70 %$ and ${T}_{2} = 300K$,

Let ${T}^{'}$ be new temperature of source

$⇒ \dfrac{7}{10} = 1 - \dfrac{300}{{T}^{'}}$

$⇒ \dfrac{300}{{T}^{'}} = 1 - \dfrac{7}{10}$

$∴ {T}^{'} = 1000K$.

questions.q: In an Isothermal change, the change in pressure and volume of a gas can be represented for three different temperature; ${T}_{3} > {T}_{2} > {T}_{1}$ as:
questions.solution:
In case of isothermal process, pressure vs volume graph is a rectangular hyperbola.

The graph of the isothermal process shifts away from the origin as the temperature of the process is increased. Thus, the curve away from the origin ${T}_{3}$ have the highest temperature whereas the curve closer to the origin ${T}_{1}$ have the lowest temperature.

Here, the dotted line shows the isobaric line that implies ${T}_{3} > {T}_{2} > {T}_{1}$ as $T = \dfrac{PV}{nR}$.

The pressure ${P}_{1}$ and density ${d}_{1}$ of diatomic gas $\left(\gamma = \dfrac{7}{5}\right)$ changes suddenly to ${P}_{2}\left(> {P}_{1}\right) and {d}_{2}$ respectively during an adiabatic process. The temperature of the gas increases and becomes____times of its initial temperature.

(given $\dfrac{{d}_{2}}{{d}_{1}} = 32$)
questions.solution:
For adiabatic process, $P{V}^{\gamma} =$ constant

We know, density $d = \dfrac{mass}{Volume}$.

Then, we have $\dfrac{P}{{d}^{\gamma}} =$ constant

Given here, $\dfrac{{d}_{2}}{{d}_{1}} = 32$ and $\gamma = \dfrac{7}{5}$.

The ratio $\dfrac{{P}_{1}}{{P}_{2}} = {\left(\dfrac{{d}_{1}}{{d}_{2}}\right)}^{\gamma} = \left(\dfrac{1}{32}\right)\dfrac{7}{5} = \dfrac{1}{128}$

The ratio of temperature using ideal gas equation is $\dfrac{{T}_{1}}{{T}_{2}} = \dfrac{{P}_{1}{V}_{1}}{{P}_{2}{V}_{2}} = \dfrac{1}{128} \times 32 = \dfrac{1}{4}$

Thus, ${T}_{2} = 4{T}_{1}$.

questions.q: At a certain temperature, the degrees of freedom per molecule for gas is $8$. The gas performs $150J$ of work when it expands under constant pressure. The amount of heat absorbed by the gas will be _____ $J$.
questions.solution:
For constant pressure process,

Work done is given by $W = nR\DeltaT = 150J$, here, $R$ is gas constant.

Now, for above process, $f = 8$.

So, specific heat at constant pressure is ${C}_{P} = \left(1 + \dfrac{f}{2}\right)R$.

Amount of heat adsorbed by the gas is

$Q = n{C}_{P}R\DeltaT = \left(\dfrac{f}{2} + 1\right)nR\DeltaT = \left(\dfrac{8}{2} + 1\right)150 = 750J$

questions.q: A Carnot engine has efficiency of $50 %$. If the temperature of sink is reduced by $40 ° C$, its efficiency increases by $30 %$. The temperature of the source will be :
questions.solution:
Initial efficiency ${η}_{0} = 50 %$, the increase in efficiency is $30 %$. Therefore, new efficiency $η = 50\left(1 + \dfrac{30}{100}\right) = 65 %$.

Efficiency of the Carnot engin is given by $η = 1 - \dfrac{{T}_{L}}{{T}_{H}}$

$⇒ {η}_{0} = \dfrac{1}{2} = 1 - \dfrac{{T}_{L}}{{T}_{H}}$

When the temperature of the sink is decreased by $40 ° C = 40K$.

$η = \dfrac{1}{2}\left(1 \cdot 3\right) = 1 - \left(\dfrac{{T}_{L} - 40}{{T}_{H}}\right)$

$⇒ \dfrac{1}{2}\left(1 \cdot 3\right) = \dfrac{1}{2} + \dfrac{40}{{T}_{H}}$

$⇒ {T}_{H} = 266 . 7K$

$η$(first case)$= η$(second case)

$⇒ {P}_{2} = 32{P}_{1}$

questions.q: A sample of an ideal gas is taken through the cyclic process $ABCA$ as shown in figure. It absorbs, $40J$ of heat during the part $AB$, no heat during $BC$ and rejects $60J$ of heat during $CA$. A work of $50J$ is done on the gas during the part $BC$. The internal energy of the gas at $A$ is $1560J$. The work done by the gas during the part $CA$ is
questions.solution:
In the part $A \to B$, the volume remains constant. Thus, the work done by the gas is zero. It is given that the heat absorbed by the gas is $40J$. From first law of thermodynamics, $Q = \DeltaU + W$

$⇒ 40 = \DeltaU + 0 ⇒ \DeltaU = 40J$

or $\DeltaU = {U}_{B} - {U}_{A} = 40J$

The increase in internal energy from $A$ to $B$ is $40J$. The internal energy is $1560J$ at $A$, then

${U}_{B} - 1560 = 40J ⇒ {U}_{B} = 1600J$

In the part $B \to C$, the work done by the gas is $W = 50J$ and no heat is given to the system. Again using $Q = \DeltaU + W$

$0 = \DeltaU - 50$ or $\DeltaU = {U}_{C} - {U}_{B} = 50J$

${U}_{C} - 1600 = 50J ⇒ {U}_{C} = 1650J$

The change in internal energy from $C \to A$,

$∆ U = 1560 - 1650 = - 90J$

The heat given to the system is $Q = - 60J$

Using $Q = \DeltaU + W$, we get $W = Q - ∆ U = - 60 - \left(- 90\right) = 30J$

questions.q:
Statement - I : When $\mu$ amount of an ideal gas undergoes adiabatic change from state $\left({P}_{1}, {V}_{1}, {T}_{1}\right)$ to state $\left({P}_{2}, {V}_{2}, {T}_{2}\right)$, then work done is $W = \dfrac{\muR\left({T}_{2} - {T}_{1}\right)}{1 - \gamma}$, where $\gamma = \dfrac{{C}_{P}}{{C}_{V}}$ and R = universal gas constant.

Statement - II : In the above case, when work is done on the gas, the temperature of the gas would rise.
options: Both statement-I and statement-II are true.
Both statement-I and statement-II are false.
Statement-I is true but statement-II is false.
Statement-I is false but statement-II is true.
questions.solution:
The work done in an adiabatic process is given by,

${W}_{adiabatic} = \dfrac{nR\left({T}_{f} - {T}_{i}\right)}{1 - \gamma} \to$ statement I is true.

For adiabatic process $∆ Q = 0$. From the first law of thermodynamics,

$∆ Q = W + \DeltaU$

$0 = W + \DeltaU$

$\DeltaU = - W$

If work is done on the gas, i.e. work is negative

$∴ \DeltaU$ is positive.

$∴$ The temperature will increase. Hence, statement II is also true.

questions.q:
A thermally insulated vessel contains an ideal gas of molecular mass $M$ and ratio of specific heats $1 . 4$. Vessel is moving with speed $v$ and is suddenly brought to rest. Assuming no heat is lost to the surrounding and vessel temperature of the gas increases by :
($R =$ universal gas constant)
questions.solution:
KE of the vessel $= \dfrac{1}{2}m{v}^{2}$

When the vessel is suddenly stopped, the ordered motion of the gas molecules is converted into disordered motion of the molecules increasing thereby the internal energy of the gas. Thus,

$∆ U = n{C}_{v} ∆ T = \dfrac{1}{2}m{v}^{2} = \dfrac{1}{2}\left(nM\right){v}^{2}$

Where $n$ is number of moles of the gas in the vessel and $M$ is molecular weight of the gas.

$∴ ∆ T = \dfrac{M{v}^{2}}{2{C}_{v}}$

As ${C}_{v} = \dfrac{R}{\gamma - 1}$

$∴ ∆ T = \dfrac{M{v}^{2} ( \gamma - 1 )}{2R} = \dfrac{M{v}^{2} ( 1 . 4 - 1 )}{2R} = \dfrac{M{v}^{2}}{5R}$

questions.q: A Carnot engine takes $5000kcal$ of heat from a reservoir at $727 ° C$ and gives heat to a sink at $127 ° C$. The work done by the engine is
questions.solution:
Given,

$Q\left(Heat\right) = 5000kcal = 5 \times {10}^{6}cal$

${T}_{2}\left(Sink\right) = {127}^{°}C = \left(127 + 273\right)K = 400K$

${T}_{1}\left(Source\right) = {727}^{°}C = \left(727 + 273\right)K = 1000K$

The efficiency of the Carnot cycle is given by,

$η = 1 - \dfrac{{T}_{sink}}{{T}_{source}} = \dfrac{W}{Q}$

$⇒ \left(1 - \dfrac{400}{1000}\right) = \dfrac{6}{10} = \dfrac{W}{5000}$⇒ W = 3000kcal$

$= 3 \times \times 4 . 2 \times {10}^{6}J = 12 . 6 \times {10}^{6}J$.

questions.q: A Carnot engine whose heat sinks at $27 ° C$, has an efficiency of $25 %$. By how many degrees should the temperature of the source be changed to increase the efficiency by $100 %$ of the original efficiency ?
questions.solution:
Efficiency of carnot engine is given by, $η = 1 - \dfrac{{T}_{sink}}{{T}_{source}}$.

For initial case: ${T}_{sink} = \left(27 + 273\right) ° C = 300K$

So we can write, $\dfrac{1}{4} = 1 - \dfrac{300}{{T}_{1}}$⇒ {T}_{1} = 400K$

Now for the second case: ${T}_{sink} = 300K$

After increasing the previous efficiency by 100%, value of efficiency will get doubled.

Therefore, $\dfrac{1}{2} = 1 - \dfrac{300}{{T}_{2}}$⇒ {T}_{2} = 600K$

Increase in temperature required will be, $600K - 400K = 200K$

questions.q: The width of one of the two slits in a Young's double slit experiment is three times the other slit. If the amplitude of the light coming from a slit is proportional to the slit-width, the ratio of minimum to maximum intensity in the interference pattern is $x: 4$ where $x$ is $_______ .$
questions.solution: Given amplitude $\propto$ slit widthAlso intensity $\propto(\text{ Amplitude })^2 \propto(\text{ Slit width })^2 \frac{I_1}{I_2}=\left(\frac{3}{1}\right)^2=9 \Rightarrow I_1=9 I_2 \frac{I_{\min }}{I_{\max }}=\left(\frac{\sqrt{I_1}-\sqrt{I_2}}{\sqrt{I_1}+\sqrt{I_2}}\right)^2=\left(\frac{3-1}{3+1}\right)^2=\frac{1}{4}=\frac{x}{4} \Rightarrow x=1$

${T}_{L} = 174K$

questions.q: A refrigerator consumes an average $35W$ power to operate between temperature $- 10 ° C$ to $25 ° C$. If there is no loss of energy then how much average heat per second does it transfer?
questions.solution:
$W + {Q}_{2} = {Q}_{1}$

$W = {Q}_{1} - {Q}_{2}$

$\dfrac{{Q}_{2}}{W} = \dfrac{{Q}_{2}}{{Q}_{1} - {Q}_{2}}$

$\dfrac{{Q}_{2}}{W} = \dfrac{{T}_{2}}{{T}_{1} - {T}_{2}}$

For one second, $W = 35J$

$\dfrac{{Q}_{2}}{35} = \dfrac{263}{298 - 263}$

${Q}_{2} = 263J$

Hence, average heat per second transferred $= 263J{s}^{- 1}$

questions.q: An electric appliance supplies $6000J{min}^{- 1}$, heat to the system. If the system delivers a power of $90W$. How long it would take to increase the internal energy by $2 . 5 \times {10}^{3}J$?
questions.solution:
Recall the formula of the first law of thermodynamics in terms of change in internal energy and work done by the system, $\DeltaU = Q - W$, given, $\DeltaU = 2500J$, $Q = \dfrac{6000}{60} \times t = \left(100t\right)J$ and $W = P \times t = 90t$,
$⇒ 2500J = 100tJ - 90tJ ⇒ t = 2 . 5 \times {10}^{2}s$.

questions.q: In thermodynamics, heat and work are :
questions.solution:
Heat and work are treated as path functions in thermodynamics.

$\DeltaQ = \DeltaU + \DeltaW$

Since work done by gas depends on type of process i.e. path and $\DeltaU$ depends just on initial and final states, so $\DeltaQ$ i.e. heat, also has to depend on process is path.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
The volume $V$ of a given mass of monoatomic gas changes with temperature $T$ according to the relation $V = KT\dfrac{2}{3}$. The workdone when temperature changes by $90K$ will be $xR$. The value of $x$ is
[$R$ universal gas constant ]
questions.solution:
We know that work done is $W = ∫ PdV . . . \left(1\right)$

$⇒ P = \dfrac{nRT}{V} . . . \left(2\right)$

$⇒ W = ∫ \dfrac{nRT}{V}dv . . . \left(3\right)$

and $V = K{T}^{2 / 3} . . . \left(4\right)$

$⇒ W = ∫ \dfrac{nRT}{K{T}^{2 / 3}} \cdot dv . . . \left(5\right)$

$⇒$ from $\left(4\right): dv = \dfrac{2}{3}K{T}^{- 1 / 3}dT$

$⇒ W = {∫}_{{T}_{1}}^{{T}_{2}}\dfrac{nRT}{K{T}^{2 / 3}}\dfrac{2}{3}K\dfrac{1}{{T}^{1 / 3}}dT$

$⇒ W = \dfrac{2}{3}nR \times \left({T}_{2} - {T}_{1}\right) . . . \left(6\right)$

$⇒ {T}_{2} - {T}_{1} = 90K . . . \left(7\right)$

$⇒ W = \dfrac{2}{3}nR \times 90$

$⇒ W = 60nR$

Assuming $1$ mole of gas

$n = 1$

So $W = 60R$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A reversible heat engine converts one-fourth of the heat input into work. When the temperature of the sink is reduced by $52K,$ its efficiency is doubled. The temperature in Kelvin of the source will be ___ .
questions.solution:
Efficiency of reversible engine is $η = \dfrac{1}{4} = \dfrac{W}{{Q}_{in}} = 1 - \dfrac{{T}_{2}}{{T}_{1}}$

From above, $\dfrac{{T}_{2}}{{T}_{1}} = \dfrac{3}{4}$

When the temperature of the sink is reduced by $52K$ then its efficiency is doubled.

Then, $\dfrac{{T}_{2} - 52}{{T}_{1}} = \dfrac{1}{2}$

$⇒ \dfrac{{T}_{2}}{{T}_{1}} - \dfrac{52}{{T}_{1}} = \dfrac{1}{2} ⇒ \dfrac{3}{4} - \dfrac{52}{{T}_{1}} = \dfrac{1}{2} ⇒ \dfrac{52}{{T}_{1}} = \dfrac{3}{4} - \dfrac{1}{2} = \dfrac{1}{4} ⇒ {T}_{1} = 52 \times 4 = 208K$

$P = k{V}^{3}$

now $PV = nRT$

$= \dfrac{200}{4} \times nR = 50nR$

questions.q: If one mole of an ideal gas at $\left({P}_{1}, {V}_{1}\right)$ is allowed to expand reversibly and isothermally ($A to B$) its pressure is reduced to one-half of the original pressure (see figure). This is followed by a constant volume cooling till its pressure is reduced to one-fourth of the initial value $\left(B \to C\right) .$ Then it is restored to its initial state by a reversible adiabatic compression ($C to A$). The net workdone by the gas is equal to:
questions.solution:
$A - B =$ isothermal process

${W}_{AB} = {P}_{1}{V}_{1}ln\left[\dfrac{2{V}_{1}}{{V}_{1}}\right] = {P}_{1}{V}_{1}ln\left(2\right)$

$B - C \to$ Isochoric process

${W}_{BC} = 0$

$C - A \to$Adiabatic process

${W}_{CA} = \dfrac{{P}_{1}{V}_{1} - \dfrac{{P}_{1}}{4} \times 2{V}_{1}}{1 - \gamma} = \dfrac{{P}_{1}{V}_{1}\left[1 - \dfrac{1}{2}\right]}{1 - \gamma} = \dfrac{{P}_{1}{V}_{1}}{2\left(1 - \gamma\right)}$

${W}_{net} = {W}_{AB} + {W}_{BC} + {W}_{CA}\left\{{P}_{1}{V}_{1} = RT\right\}$

$= {P}_{1}{V}_{1}ln\left(2\right) + 0 + \dfrac{{P}_{1}{V}_{1}}{2\left(1 - \gamma\right)}$

${W}_{net} = RT\left[ln\left(2\right) - \dfrac{1}{2\left(\gamma - 1\right)}\right]$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
$n$ mole of a perfect gas undergoes a cyclic process $ABCA$ (see figure) consisting of the following processes.

$A \to B:$ Isothermal expansion at temperature $T$ so that the volume is doubled from ${V}_{1}$ to ${V}_{2} = 2{V}_{1}$ and pressure changes from ${P}_{1}$ to ${P}_{2}$
$B \to C:$ Isobaric compression at pressure ${P}_{2}$ to initial volume ${V}_{1} .$

$C \to A:$ Isochoric change leading to change of pressure from ${P}_{2}$ to ${P}_{1}$

Total work done in the complete cycle $ABCA$ is:
questions.solution:
${W}_{isothermal} = nRT ln\left(\dfrac{{V}_{2}}{{V}_{1}}\right)$\

${W}_{isobaric} = P\DeltaV = nR\DeltaT$

${W}_{isochoric} = 0$

${W}_{1} = nRTln\left(\dfrac{2V}{V}\right) = nRTln2$

${W}_{2} = nR\left(\dfrac{T}{2} - T\right) = - nR\dfrac{T}{2}$

${W}_{3} = 0$

$⇒ {W}_{net} = {W}_{1} + {W}_{2} + {W}_{3}$

${W}_{net} = nRT\left(ln2 - \dfrac{1}{2}\right)$

questions.q: In an adiabatic process, the density of a diatomic gas becomes $32$n$ times its initial value. The final pressure of the gas is found to be $n$ times the initial pressure. The value of $n$ is:
questions.solution:
Given,

Final density of diatomic gas is ${ρ}_{f} = 32n{ρ}_{i}$

Final pressure is ${P}_{f} = n{P}_{i}$

In adiabatic process, equation of state is given by,

$P{V}^{\gamma} = \text{constant} . . . \left(1\right)$

Where, $V$ is the volume, $P$ is the pressure and $\gamma = \dfrac{7}{5}$ is the ratio of specific heat of diatomic gas

$P{\left(\dfrac{m}{ρ}\right)}^{\gamma} = \text{constant} . . . \left(2\right)$, As $V = \dfrac{m}{ρ}$

and mass is constant, then the pressure is given by

$∴ P ∝ {ρ}^{\gamma}$

$⇒ \dfrac{{P}_{f}}{{P}_{i}} = {\left(\dfrac{{ρ}_{f}}{{ρ}_{i}}\right)}^{\gamma}$

$⇒ \dfrac{n{P}_{i}}{{P}_{i}} = {\left(\dfrac{32{ρ}_{i}}{{ρ}_{i}}\right)}^{{}^{7 / 5}} = ( 32{)}^{7 / 5}$

$∴ n = {2}^{7} = 128$

and mass is constant, then the pressure is given by

$⇒ \dfrac{{P}_{f}}{{P}_{i}} = {\left(\dfrac{{ρ}_{f}}{{ρ}_{i}}\right)}^{\gamma}$

$⇒ \dfrac{n{P}_{i}}{{P}_{i}} = {\left(\dfrac{32{ρ}_{i}}{{ρ}_{i}}\right)}^{{}^{7 / 5}} = ( 32{)}^{7 / 5}$

$∴ n = {2}^{7} = 128$

Relation between the ratio of specific heat and degree of freedom is given by,

If all the processes are the quasi-static then the final temperature of the gas (in ${}^{o}K$ ) is (to the nearest integer) ___________.
questions.solution:
$P{V}^{y} = constant$
$T{V}^{- 1} = constant$
$300{\left({V}_{1}\right)}^{1.4 - 1} = {T}_{B}{\left(\dfrac{{V}_{1}}{16}\right)}^{2 / 5}$
${T}_{B} = 300 \times {2}^{8 / 5}$
Now for BC process
$\dfrac{{V}_{B}}{{T}_{B}} = \dfrac{{V}_{c}}{{T}_{c}}$
${T}_{c} = \dfrac{{V}_{c}{T}_{B}}{{v}_{B}} = 2 \times 300 \times {2}^{8 / 5}$
${T}_{c} = 1818.859$
${T}_{c} = 1819K$

Relaxation time $\left(τ\right) ∝ \dfrac{V}{\sqrt{T}}$
And $T ∝ \dfrac{1}{{V}^{\gamma - 1}}$
$τ ∝ {V}^{1 + \dfrac{\gamma - 1}{2}}$
$τ ∝ V\dfrac{1 + \gamma}{2}$
$\dfrac{{τ}_{f}}{{τ}_{i}} = {\left(\dfrac{2V}{V}\right)}^{\dfrac{\gamma + 1}{2}}$
$\dfrac{{τ}_{f}}{{τ}_{i}} = {\left(2\right)}^{\dfrac{\gamma + 1}{2}}$

questions.q: Two ideal Carnot engines operate in cascade (all heat given up by one engine is used by the other engine to produce work) between temperatures, ${T}_{1}$ and ${T}_{2}$ . The temperature of the hot reservoir of the first engine is ${T}_{1}$ and the temperature of the cold reservoir of the second engine is ${T}_{2}$ . $T$ is temperature of the sink of first engine which is also the source for the second engine. How is $T$ related to ${T}_{1}$ and ${T}_{2}$ , if both the engines perform equal amount of work?
questions.solution:
${Q}_{1}:$ Heat input to ${I}^{st}$ engine
$Q:$ Heat rejected from ${I}^{st}$ engine
${Q}_{2}:$ Heat rejected from $I{I}^{nd}$ engine
Work done by ${I}^{st}$ engine $=$ work done by $I{I}^{nd}$ engine.
$Q - {Q}_{2} = {Q}_{1} - Q$
$2Q = {Q}_{1} + {Q}_{2}$
$2 = \dfrac{{T}_{1}}{T} + \dfrac{{T}_{2}}{T}$
$\text{T} = \dfrac{{\text{T}}_{1} + {\text{T}}_{2}}{2}$

questions.q: A sample of an ideal gas is taken through the cyclic process $abca$ as shown in the figure. The change in the internal energy of the gas along the path $ca$ is $- 180J .$ The gas absorbs $250J$ of heat along the path $ab$ and $60J$ along the path $bc$ . The work done by the gas along the path $abc$ is:
questions.solution:
In a cyclic process, $\DeltaU = 0$
From 1st law of thermodynamics
$Q = \DeltaU + W$
$Q = W$
${Q}_{ab} + {Q}_{bc} + {Q}_{ca} = {W}_{abc} + {W}_{ca}$
${W}_{abc} = {Q}_{ab} + {Q}_{bc} + {Q}_{ca} - {W}_{ca}$
${W}_{abc} = {Q}_{ab} + {Q}_{bc} + {U}_{ca}$
${W}_{abc} = 250 + 60 - 180 = 130J$

questions.q: One mole of an ideal gas passes through a process where pressure and volume obey the relation $P = {P}_{o}\left[1 - \dfrac{1}{2}{\left(\dfrac{{V}_{o}}{V}\right)}^{2}\right]$ . Here ${P}_{o}$ and ${V}_{o}$ are constants. Calculate the change in the temperature of the gas if its volume changes from ${V}_{o}$ to $2{V}_{o}$ .
questions.solution:
For ideal gas, $PV = nRT$
Therefore, $\dfrac{nRT}{V} = {P}_{0}\left[1 - \dfrac{1}{2}{\left(\dfrac{{V}_{0}}{V}\right)}^{2}\right]$
$⇒ T = \dfrac{{P}_{0}V}{R}\left[1 - \dfrac{1}{2}{\left(\dfrac{{V}_{0}}{V}\right)}^{2}\right]$
Therefore, the change in temperature is:
$\DeltaT = {T}_{f} - {T}_{i}$
$= \dfrac{{P}_{0}\left({2V}_{0}\right)}{R}\left(1 - \dfrac{1}{2}{\left(\dfrac{{V}_{0}}{{2V}_{0}}\right)}^{2}\right) - \dfrac{{P}_{0}V}{R}\left(1 - \dfrac{{V}_{0}^{2}}{2{V}_{0}^{2}}\right)$
$= \dfrac{{5P}_{0}{V}_{0}}{4R}$

Therefore, the change in temperature is:
$\DeltaT = {T}_{f} - {T}_{i}$
$= \dfrac{{P}_{0}\left({2V}_{0}\right)}{R}\left(1 - \dfrac{1}{2}{\left(\dfrac{{V}_{0}}{{2V}_{0}}\right)}^{2}\right) - \dfrac{{P}_{0}V}{R}\left(1 - \dfrac{{V}_{0}^{2}}{2{V}_{0}^{2}}\right)$
$= \dfrac{{5P}_{0}{V}_{0}}{4R}$

questions.q: $n$ moles of an ideal gas with constant volume heat capacity ${C}_{v}$ undergo an isobaric expansion by certain volume. The ratio of the work done in the process, to the heat supplied is:
questions.solution:
From First Law of thermodynamics,
$\DeltaQ = \DeltaU + \Deltaw$
$\dfrac{\Deltaw}{\DeltaQ} = 1 - \dfrac{\DeltaU}{\DeltaQ} = 1 - \dfrac{n{c}_{v}\DeltaT}{n{c}_{p}\DeltaT}$
$= 1 - \dfrac{{c}_{v}}{R + {c}_{v}}$
$= \dfrac{R}{R + {c}_{v}}$
As, $n{c}_{v} = {C}_{v}$
$\dfrac{\Deltaw}{\DeltaQ} = \dfrac{nR}{{C}_{v} + nR}$

The first one, $A,$ receives heat at ${T}_{1}\left(= 600K\right)$ and rejects to a reservoir at temperature ${T}_{2} .$ The second engine $B$ receives heat rejected by the first engine and, in turn, rejects to a heat reservoir at ${T}_{3}\left(= 400K\right) .$ Calculate the temperature ${T}_{2}$ if the work outputs of the two engines are equal:

$W = {Q}_{1} - {Q}_{2} = {Q}_{2} - {Q}_{3}$

$\dfrac{{T}_{1}}{{T}_{2}} + \dfrac{{T}_{3}}{{T}_{2}} = 2$

For path $ADB$

$\Delta Q = \Delta U + \Delta W$

As initial and find points are the same, change in internal energy is same in both the cases

$\Delta Q = 30 + 10$

$= 40J$

Work done in cycle $=$area under closed curve

Heat given $= {Q}_{AB} + {Q}_{BC}$

$= \dfrac{13}{2}{P}_{0}{V}_{0}$

Thermal efficiency, $η = \dfrac{W}{{Q}_{absorbed}} = \dfrac{2}{13} = 0.15$

questions.solution:
Temperature $T$ will be maximum where product of $PV$ is max equation of line

$PV = - \dfrac{{P}_{0}}{{V}_{0}}{V}^{2} + 3{P}_{0}V$

For maxima, $\dfrac{d ( PV )}{dV} = 0$

$⇒ T = \dfrac{PV}{nR} = \dfrac{9{P}_{0} {V}_{0}}{4 nR}$

Alternate method :

Since initial and final temperature are equal.

Hence maximum temperature is at middle of line.

$PV = nR{T}_{max}$

$⇒ {T}_{max} = \dfrac{\left(\dfrac{3{P}_{0}}{2}\right)\left(\dfrac{3{V}_{0}}{2}\right)}{nR} = \dfrac{9{P}_{0}{V}_{0}}{4nR}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
Consider an ideal gas confined in an isolated closed chamber. As the gas undergoes an adiabatic expansion, the average time of collision between molecules increases as ${V}^{q}$ , where $V$ is the volume of the gas. The value of $q$ is:

$\left(\gamma = \dfrac{{C}_{P}}{{C}_{v}}\right)$
questions.solution:
For an adiabatic process $T{V}^{\gamma - 1} =$ constant.
We know that average time of collision between molecules

$τ = \dfrac{1}{n\pi\sqrt{2}{v}_{rms}{d}^{2}}$

where, $n =$ number of molecules per unit volume ${V}_{rms} =$ rms velocity of molecules

As $n ∝ \dfrac{1}{V}$ and ${v}_{rms} ∝ \sqrt{T}$

$τ ∝ \dfrac{V}{\sqrt{T}}$

Thus, we can write

$n = {K}_{1}{V}^{- 1}$ and ${V}_{rms} = {K}_{2}T\dfrac{1}{2}$.

where, ${K}_{1}$ and ${K}_{2}$ are constants.

For adiabatic process, $T{V}^{\gamma - 1} =$ constant. Thus, we can write

$τ ∝ V{T}^{- \dfrac{1}{2}} ∝ V\left({V}^{1 - \gamma}\right)\dfrac{- 1}{2}$

or $τ ∝ V\dfrac{\gamma + 1}{2}$

questions.q: Consider a spherical shell of radius R at temperature T. The black body radiation inside it can be considered as an ideal gas of photons with internal energy per unit volume $u = \dfrac{U}{V} ∝ {T}^{4}$ and pressure $p = \dfrac{1}{3}\left(\dfrac{U}{V}\right)$ . If the shell now undergoes an adiabatic expansion the relation between T and R is:
questions.solution:
$∵$ in an adiabatic process.

$Q = 0$

So by first law of thermodynamics

$Q = dU + W$

$⇒ 0 = dU + W$

$⇒ W = - dU$

$∴ W = PdV$

$⇒ PdV = - dU$ ....(i)

Given that $\dfrac{U}{V} ∝ {T}^{4} ⇒ U = kV{T}^{4}$

$⇒ dU = kd\left(V{T}^{4}\right) = K\left({T}^{4}dV + 4{T}^{3}VdT\right)$

Also, $P = \dfrac{1}{3}\dfrac{U}{V} = \dfrac{1}{3}\dfrac{kV{T}^{4}}{V} = \dfrac{K{T}^{4}}{3}$

Putting these values in equation (i)

$⇒ \dfrac{K{T}^{4}}{3}dV = - k\left({T}^{4}dV + 4{T}^{3}VdT\right)$

$⇒ \dfrac{TdV}{3} = - TdV - 4VdT$

$⇒ \dfrac{4T}{3}dV = - 4VdT$

$⇒ \dfrac{1}{3}\dfrac{dV}{V} = - \dfrac{dT}{T}$

$⇒ \dfrac{1}{3}ln ⁡ V = - ln ⁡ T ⇒ ln ⁡ V = ln ⁡ {T}^{- 3}$

$⇒ V{T}^{3} = \text{constant}$

$\dfrac{4}{3}\pi{R}^{3}{T}^{3} = \text{constant}$

$RT = \text{constant}$

$⇒ T ∝ \dfrac{1}{R}$

questions.q: A solid body of constant heat capacity $1J{\left(℃\right)}^{- 1}$ is being heated by keeping it in contact with reservoirs in two ways: (i) Sequentially keeping in contact with 2 reservoirs such that each reservoir supplies the same amount of heat. (ii) Sequentially keeping in contact with $8$ reservoirs such that each reservoir supplies the same amount of heat. In both, cases the body is brought from initial temperature $100K$ to final temperature $200K$ . Entropy change of the body in the two cases respectively is: Note: This question was awarded as a bonus since temperatures were given in centigrade instead of in Kelvin. Proper corrections are made in the question to avoid it.
questions.solution:
Change in entropy,

$\begin{array}{ll}dS = \dfrac{dQ}{T} \\ \DeltaQ = \text{heat}\text{supplied} = C\DeltaT{ C = J{\left(° C\right)}^{- 1} } \\ dQ = Cdt \\ dS = \dfrac{CdT}{T} \\ \text{Intergrating}\text{both}\text{sides} \\ \mathop{∫}_{{S}_{i}}^{{S}_{f}}dS = C ∫ \dfrac{dT}{T} \\ ⇒ {S}_{f} - {S}_{i} = \DeltaS = C . lnT{|}_{100}^{200} \\ ⇒ \DeltaS = C[ ln200 - ln100 ] = Cln2 \\ \text{and}C = J{\left(° C\right)}^{- 1} \\ ⇒ \DeltaS = ln2 \\ \text{Entrpoy change in same for both cases as C is constant, and} \\ \text{temperature change (i}\text{.e}\text{. from 100 to 200) is same}\text{.}\end{array}$

questions.q: A monoatomic gas is compressed from a volume of $2{m}^{3}$ to a volume of $1{m}^{3}$ at a constant pressure of $100N{m}^{2}$. Then it is heated at constant volume by supplying $150J$ of energy. As a result, the internal energy of the gas
questions.solution:
Isobaric process with $Q = 0$

$∴ 0 = \text{W} + \Delta \text{U}$

$∴ 0 = \text{P} \Delta \text{V} + \Delta \text{U}$

$∴ \Delta \text{U} = - \text{P} \Delta \text{V}$

$= - 100\left\{1 - 2\right\}\text{J}$

$\Delta \text{U} = 100\text{J}$

Constant volume with $Q = 150J$

$\text{Q} = 0 + \Delta \text{U}$

$∴ \Delta {\text{U}}_{2} = 150 J$

$∴ \Delta \text{U} = \Delta {\text{U}}_{1} + \Delta {\text{U}}_{2}$

$= + 2 5 0 J$

Hence, internal energy increases by $250J$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A Carnot engine absorbs $1000 \mathrm{~J}$ of heat energy from a reservoir at $127^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ and rejects $600 \mathrm{~J}$ of heat energy during each cycle. The efficiency of engine and temperature of sink will be:
questions.solution:
Given: $\mathrm{Q}_1=1000 \mathrm{~J}$$
\begin{aligned}
&\mathrm{Q}_2=600 \mathrm{~J} \\
&\mathrm{~T}_1=127^{\circ} \mathrm{C}=400 \mathrm{~K} \\
&\mathrm{~T}_2=? \\
&\eta=?
\end{aligned}
$
Efficiency of carnot engine,
$
\begin{aligned}
&\eta=\frac{W}{Q_1} \times 100 \% \\
&\text{ or, } \eta=\frac{Q_2-Q_1}{Q_1} \times 100 \%
\end{aligned}
$
or, $\eta=\frac{\mathrm{Q}_2-\mathrm{Q}_1}{\mathrm{Q}_1} \times 100 \%$
or, $\eta=\frac{1000-600}{1000} \times 100 \%$$
\eta=40 \%
$
Now, for carnot cycle $\frac{\mathrm{Q}_2}{\mathrm{Q}_1}=\frac{\mathrm{T}_2}{\mathrm{~T}_1}$$
\begin{aligned}
&\frac{600}{1000}=\frac{\mathrm{T}_2}{400} \\
&\mathrm{~T}_2=\frac{600 \times 400}{1000}=240 \mathrm{~K}=240-273 \\
&\therefore \mathrm{T}_2=-33^{\circ} \mathrm{C}
\end{aligned}
$

questions.solution:
Given : work done, $W=830 \mathrm{~J}$
No. of moles of gas, $\mu=2$
For diatomic gas $\gamma=1.4$
Work done during an adiabatic change

$\begin{aligned}$&W=$\frac{\mu R\left(T_1-T_2\right)}{\gamma-1}$\\

&\Rightarrow $\Delta T=\frac{830 \times 0.4}{2 \times 8.3}$=$20 \mathrm{~K}
\end{aligned}$

questions.q: The equation of state for a gas is given by $\text{PV} = \text{nRT} + \alpha \text{V}$, where n is the number of moles and $\alpha$  is a positive constant. The initial temperature and pressure of one mole of the gas contained in a cylinder are T<sub>0</sub> and P<sub>0</sub> respectively. The work done by the gas when its temperature doubles isobarically will be :
questions.solution:
$\text{PV} = \text{nRT} + α \text{V}$

$\dfrac{{\text{P}_{0} \text{dV}}{\text{dT}} = \text{R} + α \dfrac{\text{dV}}{\text{dT}}$

$\left({\text{P}_{0} - α\right) \dfrac{\text{dV}}{\text{dT}} = \text{R}$

$∴ \text{dV} = \dfrac{\text{RdT}}{{\text{P}_{0} - α}$

$∴ \text{W} = ∫ {P}_{0} \text{dV} = \mathop{∫}_{{\text{T}_{0}}^{2 {\text{T}_{0}} \dfrac{{\text{P}_{0} \text{R}}{{\text{P}_{0} - α} \text{dT}$

$= \dfrac{{\text{P}_{0} {\text{T}_{0} \text{R}}{{\text{P}_{0} - α}$

The efficiency of cycle is
